Interiority is the private inner world that exists inside a person — everything that happens in their mind and heart that no one else can directly see. It includes their thoughts, feelings, memories, desires, fears, imagination, self-awareness, and the quiet, ongoing experience of simply being alive as themselves.

Think of it this way: everything you show the world — your words, actions, expressions — is your exterior. Everything happening inside you, invisible to others, is your interiority.

Interiority isn't one single thing. It's the sum of a person's whole inner world:

  • The thoughts running through your head in a quiet moment
  • Emotions you feel but never say out loud
  • The way you silently interpret what's happening around you
  • Private fears, hopes, doubts, and memories
  • Your ongoing sense of who you are and how you see yourself

The defining quality of interiority is that it is yours and private. Another person can watch you, study you, and know you well — but they can never directly access your interiority. They only ever see its effects.

Those words are narrower. "Thoughts" are specific and discrete. "Feelings" are emotional. But "interiority" names the entire landscape of someone's inner existence as one unified thing — the conscious and the half-conscious, the clear and the murky, the felt and the imagined, all together. It implies depth, complexity, and an inescapable privacy.

It also carries a slight philosophical weight: it acknowledges that a person isn't just a body acting in the world but a subject — someone with an inner dimension that is fundamentally their own.
Where you'll most commonly encounter this word

1. Literature and storytelling — this is by far the most common context.

When writers and critics talk about interiority in fiction, they mean: how much access does this story give us to what a character experiences inside?

A novel or story with rich interiority puts you inside a character's head. You don't just observe what they do — you experience their private thoughts, inner conflicts, and emotional reactions in real time. You know why they hesitated before speaking, what they really felt in a moment no one else witnessed, and what is going on beneath the surface of every scene.

A story with little or no interiority keeps you on the surface. You only see actions and dialogue — what characters do and say — but the inner world stays hidden. The characters feel opaque, like people you're watching through a glass wall. You can see them, but you can't know them.

Techniques writers use to create interiority:

  • Stream of consciousness — writing that mimics the raw, unfiltered flow of a character's thoughts (used memorably by Virginia Woolf and James Joyce). It feels messy and associative, because real thought is.
  • Interior monologue — longer, more organized passages of a character's inner thoughts, often written in first person even within a third-person story.
  • Free indirect discourse — a subtler technique where the narrator's voice blends with the character's inner voice. There's no "she thought" tag; the character's perspective seeps directly into the narration, so you feel you're reading from inside their mind without being told you are.

Examples of the word in use:

  • "The novel's greatest strength is its interiority — we feel every flicker of the protagonist's doubt."
  • "The film lacks interiority; the characters never come alive because we never know what's happening inside them."
  • "She writes with remarkable interiority, giving us full access to her narrator's deepest anxieties."

Here, interiority points to the simple but profound fact that conscious beings have a subjective inner experience — there is "something it is like" to be you, from the inside, that cannot be fully shared or transferred to another person.

You can describe pain to someone. You can even describe it perfectly. But the other person cannot feel your pain. That irreducible gap between the outer world and your inner experience is what philosophers mean when they speak of interiority. It's the hard problem of consciousness in a single word.

In psychology, the term can describe how reflective and emotionally complex a person is — the depth and richness of their inner life.

Critics sometimes use "interiority" to describe works of art — paintings, music, film — that seem to turn inward rather than outward. A piece with interiority evokes an inner emotional or mental state rather than simply depicting the external world.

"There is a quiet interiority to her paintings — they seem to capture a state of mind, not just a scene."

People and characters are often described as having more or less interiority — meaning a richer or shallower inner life, or a narrative that gives us more or less access to that life.

  • "A character of great interiority" — someone whose inner world is complex, vivid, layered
  • "A character with little interiority" — someone who seems to exist only on the surface; you never get the sense of a life happening inside them
  • "The author gives us direct access to the character's interiority" — we can read their innermost thoughts and feelings
  • "The story deliberately withholds interiority" — the author keeps us outside the character's head, creating mystery or emotional distance as a stylistic choice

Interiority is the private, subjective inner world of a person — all their thoughts, feelings, memories, desires, and self-awareness considered as a whole — and in literature especially, it refers to how deeply a story takes us inside that world.
